name: Phytosphingosine
lead: Phytosphingosine is an 18-carbon sphingoid base (2-aminooctadecane-1,3,4-triol) abundant in plants and fungi and also present in animals. It is a building block of more complex sphingolipids, including certain ceramides [1][2].

In skincare it is added to moisturisers, cleansers and blemish-prone-skin products as a ceramide precursor. The idea behind these products is that supplying skin-type lipids supports the stratum corneum barrier, which people associate with smoother, calmer, less dry-looking skin. Ceramide composition of skin scale has been studied in skin disease, which is why barrier lipids are a common target of cosmetic formulation [3].

Research on phytosphingosine itself is mostly laboratory work on sphingolipid metabolism, yeast biology and cell studies. No human trial of topical phytosphingosine for appearance outcomes was found; related work in humans covers barrier-lipid emollients as a category and an oral supplement study in metabolic syndrome [6][7].

paras: The outermost layer of skin, the stratum corneum, is often described as bricks and mortar: flattened cells are held together by a lipid matrix. That matrix is made of ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids in roughly equal molar proportions, with ceramides making up about half by weight, and it limits evaporative water loss while helping block microorganisms.[13]

Ceramide structures differ by body site, a difference linked to variations in skin thickness and flexibility, such as thin facial skin compared with thick heel skin.[13] In inflammatory skin conditions the ceramide profile shifts: studies of psoriasis reported more of some ceramide classes and fewer of others, which may weaken the water barrier, and the ceramide composition of psoriatic scale was described in a 1993 paper.[3][13] Dry or polluted air, harsh sulfates, excessive heat, ultraviolet exposure and ageing are described as factors that can lower ceramide levels.[13]

This is the context in which phytosphingosine appears in cosmetics. Because it is a sphingoid base that cells convert into ceramides,[2] formulators add it, and ceramides themselves, to soaps, shampoos, skin creams and sunscreens, and ceramide ingredients have undergone a Cosmetic Ingredient Review safety assessment.[13] Proponents of barrier-focused routines say replenishing these lipids leaves skin looking smoother and less dry; the published trials of ceramide-type lipids concern the blends rather than phytosphingosine alone.[6]

Wikipedia lists the compound's melting point as 102-103 C and flags eye-damage and environmental hazard classifications for the pure chemical.[1] Sphingolipid synthesis, in which sphingoid bases like phytosphingosine are converted to ceramides, has been mapped in detail, including in yeast where phytosphingosine-based ceramides are prominent.[2][4]

Ceramide composition of skin scale has been studied in disease; a 1993 paper described the ceramide composition of psoriatic scale, an example of how skin lipid profiles are linked to barrier health.[3]

Phytosphingosine is released when enzymes called ceramidases break down phytoceramide, alongside a free fatty acid; the alkaline ceramidase family was first identified in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae and later found in other species [12]. Reviews of sphingolipid structural variants note that most work has historically studied the common 18-carbon monounsaturated backbone, with less attention to variants such as phytosphingosine-based species [8]. In plants, fungi and protozoa, ceramides built on phytosphingosine are widespread [9]. Wikipedia gives its CAS number as 554-62-1 and a GHS signal word of Danger for the pure chemical, with corrosive and environmental hazard pictograms [1].

Laboratory studies cited by Wikipedia report that phytosphingosine induced programmed cell death in human cancer cells (2003) and showed T-cell-related anti-inflammatory properties in inflammatory bowel disease models (2021).[1] These are not skin-appearance findings.

A 2005 study reported that phytosphingosine induced mitochondria-involved apoptosis in cancer cells [10]. Dental researchers have examined phytosphingosine applied with tooth brushing in an in vitro and in situ study using bovine enamel, reporting changes in colour stability, roughness and microhardness [11].
No studies found on phytosphingosine for skin appearance. A registered trial of skin barrier function and inflammation in ageing exists but its link to phytosphingosine is not established [5].

Related human research is limited to other materials and routes. A 2025 double-blind intraparticipant trial of 58 adults with a history of eczema compared a multivesicular emulsion containing physiological lipids and glycerine against a glycerine emulsion over 28 days. Barrier integrity improved at the lipid-treated sites, while the comparison emollient reduced dryness without improving the barrier. This tested a physiological lipid blend, not phytosphingosine alone [6].

A 2010 double-blind crossover study gave oral phytosphingosine (500 mg twice daily) or placebo to 12 men with metabolic syndrome for four weeks each. It reported lower total cholesterol and improved insulin sensitivity without a change in body weight or fat mass [7].

card.summary: A plant- and yeast-derived ceramide building block added to barrier and blemish skincare; cosmetic trials are lacking.
card.note: Thin source base; claims rest on general ceramide biology.

quick.overview:
Phytosphingosine is a fatty-chain amino alcohol that cells use to build ceramides, lipids central to the skin barrier. It appears in some moisturisers and acne-prone skin products.
No human studies of it as a cosmetic exist.
quick.mechanism: It is a precursor in sphingolipid and ceramide synthesis; the idea behind skincare use is to supply raw material for barrier lipids.
quick.risks: No cosmetic safety trials were found. The pure chemical carries eye-damage and environmental hazard classifications per Wikipedia.

chain: Phytosphingosine is a sphingoid base that cells convert into ceramides
Skincare products supply it to support the skin's lipid barrier
A stronger barrier is associated with less dryness and irritation, and calmer-looking skin
angle.text: People use phytosphingosine in barrier and blemish-prone skincare as a ceramide building block, hoping for better hydration and a calmer, smoother complexion. The mechanism rests on general ceramide biology rather than studies of phytosphingosine itself.
